183-day-rule-by-state.html.text:
← State residency day counter

The 183-day rule by state, with a worked example

People who work remotely, split the year between two homes or travel for months at a time keep running into the same question: how many days can I spend in a state before it treats me as a resident? Several states answer it with a day count, and a mistake is expensive because a resident is taxed on all income, not only what was earned there.

Open the free day counter

A worked example

An invented remote employee spends January to March in Florida, April to the end of August in New York, a fortnight in New Jersey, mid-September to October in New York again and finishes the year in Florida. They keep a home in New York.

StateDaysAgainst the commonly published test
New York198Over the 183-day limit by 15, with an abode in the state
Florida151No wage income tax
New Jersey16No abode there, so the day test does not apply

The counter also shows that by 30 September they had 167 New York days and would have crossed the line on 17 October had they stayed every day from then on. Cutting the second New York stay short by 15 days is what keeps them under, and that is the kind of decision the room-left column is for. Whether the stay can be shortened, and whether the home counts as an abode, are questions for a tax professional, not for a calculator.

Check your own year

Questions

Is it 183 days or more than 183 days?

In the statutory tests that publish a number, the trigger is more than 183 days, so 183 days is still under the line and 184 crosses it. In a non-leap year that is just over half of 365 days. The counter treats the limit the same way and shows how many days of room are left.

Does a 183-day count make me a resident on its own?

No. The statutory tests that use 183 days usually also need a permanent place of abode in the state, and states that decide residency by domicile can treat you as a resident with far fewer days. A day count is one input, which is why the counter only marks a statutory state over the limit when you say you keep a home there.

Which states use a day count?

Commonly cited examples are New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Rhode Island, Virginia, Maryland and Utah (183 days or more), Michigan, Vermont and Maine at more than 183 days with an abode, Georgia at 183 days or more with no abode needed (over the trailing 365 days), Oregon at more than 200 and Idaho at more than 270. California is domicile based with a presumption linked to time spent in the state. States without a wage income tax, such as Florida, Texas and Nevada, have no wage-tax residency question at all, though other tests can apply. Check the state's current guidance before relying on this list.

california-nine-month-residency-presumpt.text:
← State residency day counter

California: the nine-month presumption, not a 183-day rule

People who split a year between California and a home in Nevada, Texas or Washington often plan around “183 days”. California does not work that way. Its residency test turns on domicile and where your connections are strongest, and published guidance describes more than nine months in the state as a presumption of residency you would have to rebut. The counter models that as a limit of about 270 days.

Open the free day counter

Three invented years

Each person is a Nevada resident who spends the start of tax year 2025 in California, counting the arrival and departure day.

California staysCA daysAgainst the 270-day line
1 January to 26 September2691 day of room
1 January to 27 September270No room left
1 January to 30 September273Over by 3

The line is a presumption, so even 269 days is not a clearance and the first row says only that the counter has not flagged it. A person with a California house, family and job can be a resident on far fewer days.

Check your own year

Questions

Is there a 183-day rule in California?

California does not use a bright-line 183-day test the way New York does. Residency turns on domicile and where your connections are strongest, and the Franchise Tax Board's published guidance describes spending more than nine months in the state as a presumption of residency that you can try to rebut. Check the FTB's own guidance.

How many days is nine months?

About 270. The counter uses 270 as the most you can spend before it flags the presumption, so 270 days shows no room left and 271 shows over. Calendar months differ in length, so this is an approximation, not the FTB's arithmetic.

Does staying under nine months mean I am not a resident?

No. The nine-month figure is a presumption, not a safe harbor. A person who keeps a home, family, work and bank accounts in California can be a resident on fewer days, and the counter cannot weigh those connections. A day count is one input to a conversation with a tax professional.

Does the arrival day count?

The counter defaults to counting any part of a day, so the arrival and departure days both count. Counting nights only gives one fewer day per stay. Plan on the conservative reading unless the state says otherwise.

index.html.text:
STATE RESIDENCY DAY COUNTER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

How many days have I spent in each state, and am I near the 183-day line?

List where you were and when. The counter totals the days per state, checks them against the commonly published statutory residency tests, shows the room you have left and the date you would cross a limit, splits remote-work wages by workdays, and gives you a day-range record to keep.

An organising aid, not tax or legal advice: residency also turns on domicile and your ties, which a day count cannot settle. New to this? Read the 183-day rule by state, with a worked example, how the convenience-of-the-employer rule can tax remote days, how many days a Florida snowbird can spend in New York, why Maryland and Utah cap you at 182 days, or how California's nine-month presumption differs from a 183-day rule.

1. The year

2. Where you were

3. Homes and limits

Enter your stays, then click Count my days.

Result

StateDaysTo as-of dateLimitRoom leftStatusWould cross onWorkdaysWages

Planning a trip? See what it would change

Add a trip to the stays above without saving it: it shows the days it adds to each state, whether it crosses a published limit, and the longest trip from that start date that stays within the limit.

How it is calculated

Days: every date in the year is checked against your stays. A day counts for a state if any stay in that state covers it; the arrival and departure days both count unless you choose to count nights. Two states can share a travel day. Overlaps that are more than a travel day are flagged as a probable typo and counted in both.

Limits: the table of commonly published tests is: a permanent place of abode plus more than 183 days for New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Rhode Island, Virginia, Maryland and Utah (183 days or more), Michigan, Vermont and Maine; 183 days or more with no home required for Georgia (counted over the trailing 365 days, which this tool approximates with the calendar year); more than 200 days for Oregon; more than 270 days for Idaho; and for California a presumption of residency beyond about nine months. A statutory state is only marked over the limit when you say you keep a home there. You can type your own limit for any state. Rules change; check the state's current guidance.

Would cross on: the date you would pass the limit if you were in the state every day from the as-of date onward.

Workdays: Monday to Friday days, split evenly across the states worked on a shared day, as a share of all workdays; the wage figure applies that share to the wages you typed. Holidays and weekends worked are not modelled. Name your employer's state to see the convenience-of-the-employer view for the states commonly described as applying it (NY, NE, DE, AR; PA, NJ and CT against states that do the same).

Not modelled: domicile, where your family and belongings are, what counts as a permanent place of abode, part-year resident rules, reciprocity agreements, city taxes, foreign days, and state-specific ways of counting a day. The counts are checked against an independent recount in the test suite, but unverified against any tax authority's own determination.

Common questions

How many days can I spend in a state before I become a tax resident?

There is no single number. Several states, including New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Rhode Island, Virginia, Maryland and Utah (183 days or more), Michigan, Vermont and Maine, publish a statutory test: you are treated as a resident if you keep a permanent place of abode there and spend more than 183 days in the state. Oregon uses 200 days and Idaho 270. Many other states, California among them, decide residency by domicile and where your ties are strongest, so a day count alone does not settle it. The counter shows where you stand against the commonly published day tests and lets you enter your own limit.

Does the day I arrive or leave count?

Often yes. New York, for example, counts any part of a day spent in the state as a day. The counter defaults to that conservative reading and counts both the arrival day and the departure day. You can switch to counting nights, which drops the departure day, but check what your state says before relying on it.

What is a permanent place of abode?

Broadly, a home you keep and could use, whether you own or rent it, as opposed to a hotel stay or a short visit to relatives. Because the statutory tests usually need both the abode and the day count, the counter only flags a statutory state as over the limit when you tell it you keep a home there. Whether a particular dwelling counts is a question for the state's own guidance or a tax professional.

What if I am a resident of two states?

It happens, usually when one state treats you as domiciled there and another treats you as a statutory resident. The usual relief is a credit on the return of the state where you are a resident for tax paid to the other, which is why people who live partly in two states keep a day-by-day record. The counter produces that record and a CSV to keep.

How are my wages split between states when I work remotely while travelling?

Many states tax wages for work physically done in the state, and an employer's allocation often follows days worked. The counter estimates a share by counting Monday to Friday workdays in each state, splitting a shared travel day evenly, and applying it to the annual wages you type. It ignores holidays and your employer's own rules, and some states have a convenience-of-the-employer rule that can pull remote work back to the employer's state, so treat the figure as an estimate to discuss with a payroll or tax professional.

Can I use this to prove where I was to a tax authority?

It builds an organised record from dates you enter, which is a good start for the contemporaneous log auditors ask for, but it is not evidence by itself. Keep what supports the dates: travel receipts, card statements, calendar entries and phone or toll records. Nothing you type is stored or uploaded, so download the CSV and keep your own copy.

Is my travel history uploaded anywhere?

No. Everything is calculated in your browser from what you type, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and it works offline once the page has loaded.

The rules are summarised from commonly published tests and may be out of date or incomplete. Counts are a record of the dates you typed.

maryland-utah-182-day-limit.html.text:
← State residency day counter

Maryland and Utah: why 183 days is already too many

Most abode-plus-days tests read “more than 183 days”, which makes 183 safe. Maryland’s reads “183 days or more” (Tax-General 10-101), and Utah’s reads the same way (Utah Code 59-10-103). In those two states the safe maximum is 182, and a person who plans around the usual 183 lands one day over.

Open the free day counter

Three invented summers

Each person is a Florida resident who keeps a Maryland home, tax year 2025, counting the arrival and departure day.

Maryland staysMD daysAgainst the 182-day limit
1 May to 28 October1811 day of room
1 May to 29 October182No room left
1 June to 30 November183Over by 1

The third row is a tidy six-month stay that most people would call safe. It is 183 days, which is exactly the number that trips Maryland’s wording. A 1 May to 31 October summer is 184, over by 2. Counting nights only, the same 1 June to 30 November stay is 182, so the departure day decides which side of the line you are on.

Check your own summer

Questions

How many days can I spend in Maryland without becoming a resident?

The commonly published statutory test makes you a Maryland resident for tax if you keep a place of abode there for more than six months and are physically present for 183 days or more. So the most you can spend and stay under the line is 182 days. Domicile is a separate test: if Maryland is your permanent home, days do not matter. Check the Comptroller's own guidance.

Why is Maryland 182 days when most states say 183?

Most states with an abode-plus-days test say residents are those who spend more than 183 days, so 183 is safe. Maryland's wording is 183 days or more, so the 183rd day is the one that crosses. Utah's statute reads the same way. The counter stores both as a limit of 182 and flags 183 as over.

Does the arrival day count?

The counter defaults to counting any part of a day, so both the arrival day and the departure day count. If you count nights only, a 1 May to 29 October stay is 181 days instead of 182. Plan on the conservative reading unless the state says otherwise.

Does a vacation home make me a Maryland resident?

Not by itself. The abode has to be one you keep for more than six months, and you also have to be present for 183 days or more. Fewer days means the statutory test does not apply, although domicile can still make you a resident. The counter only does the day arithmetic.

remote-work-convenience-of-the-employer-.text:
← State residency day counter

Working remotely from another state: the convenience-of-the-employer rule, with numbers

The usual advice is that a state taxes wages for work done inside it. A handful of states add a twist: if you work from home in another state for an employer located in theirs, they can still treat those days as worked at the employer's office, unless the employer required you to be elsewhere. For someone who moved to a state with no wage tax, that is the difference between paying nothing on those days and paying the employer's state on all of them.

Open the free day counter

A worked example

The same invented year as the 183-day guide: a Florida-based employee on a $140,000 salary whose employer is in New York. They spend 132 workdays physically in New York and 107 in Florida (239 workdays in all, weekdays only, holidays not modelled).

ReadingWorkdays claimed by New YorkWages New York may claim
Physical location only132$77,322
Convenience-of-the-employer rule applies239$140,000

The 107 Florida workdays carry $62,678 of pay. Florida has no wage income tax, so there is no Florida return on which to claim a credit for what New York collects on it: the exposure is not offset. Whether the rule applies depends on whether the employer required the Florida work, which a calculator cannot tell and a payroll or tax professional can.

Check your own year

Questions

What is the convenience-of-the-employer rule?

A rule used by a few states, commonly listed as New York, Nebraska, Delaware and Arkansas, under which days you work from home outside the state for an employer located in the state are still treated as in-state workdays unless the employer required you to work elsewhere. Allowing remote work is not the same as requiring it. Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Connecticut are commonly described as applying the rule only against residents of states that apply it to them. Check the state's current guidance.

If I live in a state with no income tax, can my employer's state still tax my wages?

It can try, under the rule above. A state with no wage income tax, such as Florida or Texas, gives you no return on which to claim a credit for tax paid to the employer's state, so the exposure is not offset. This is the case where the rule costs the most and the reason to keep a workday record.

What do I do about it?

Keep a day-by-day record of where you worked, ask your employer whether the work location is required for the job or a personal choice, ask payroll how wages are being allocated, and speak to a tax professional before filing. The counter shows the days and the wages each reading would claim; it does not decide which reading applies to you.

snowbird-days-in-new-york.html.text:
← State residency day counter

Florida snowbird: how many days can you spend in New York?

Many people live in Florida for the winter and keep a home in New York for the summer. New York's statutory test treats someone who keeps a permanent place of abode in the state as a resident if they spend more than 183 days there, counting any part of a day. The trap is that a natural six-month summer is one day too long.

Open the free day counter

Three invented summers

Each person is a Florida resident with a New York home, tax year 2025, counting the arrival and departure day.

New York staysNY daysAgainst the 183-day test
1 May to 31 October184Over by 1
1 May to 30 September15330 days of room
15 May to 10 October, plus 20 to 31 December16122 days of room

The first row is the one people miss: May through October is six calendar months, and with both end days counted it is 184 days. Counting nights only (dropping the departure day) it is 183, which sits exactly on the line with no room, so even the lenient reading leaves nothing to spare. The third row shows why a holiday trip home matters: the December visit costs 12 days of the 34 the person would otherwise have left.

Check your own summer

Questions

How many days can a Florida snowbird spend in New York?

If you keep a permanent place of abode in New York, the statutory test treats you as a resident once you spend more than 183 days there, counting any part of a day. So 183 days is the most you can spend and stay under the line, and a six-month summer from 1 May to 31 October is 184 days. Without a New York abode the day test does not apply, but New York can still treat you as a domiciliary if your ties are there. Check the state's own guidance.

Does leaving Florida make me a New York resident?

Not by that fact alone. Residency turns on domicile (where you intend to make your permanent home) and, separately, on the abode-plus-days statutory test. Spending fewer than 184 days in New York does not by itself prove you changed domicile, which is why people who move south also keep records of where their ties are. The counter only does the day arithmetic.

Should I count nights or days?

New York counts any part of a day spent in the state as a day, so the arrival day and the departure day both count. The counter defaults to that inclusive reading. On the nights reading the 1 May to 31 October summer is 183 days, which looks safe, but only the state's rule decides which reading applies, so plan on the conservative one.

What should I keep to back up my day count?

A contemporaneous day-by-day log, plus what supports it: travel receipts and boarding passes, card statements, toll and phone records, and calendar entries. The counter prints a day-by-day log with a blank evidence column and exports it as CSV so you can fill it in as you go.
